meta.title: Who really said "Give the People What They Want and They'll Come"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Goodman Ace, but Ace was quoting George Jessel — and said so. A showbiz joke about a well-attended funeral, traced to the 1940s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Give the People What They Want and They'll Come'?
meta.ogDescription: Goodman Ace printed it in 1955 — while crediting George Jessel. Quote Investigator credits Jessel. The provenance, with sources.

answer.label: Not Goodman Ace — actually George Jessel
answer.authorDates: 3 April 1898 – 23 May 1981 · American vaudeville comedian, actor & toastmaster
answer.sourceLine: The line is a mordant showbiz joke: a hated movie mogul’s funeral draws an enormous crowd, and someone explains it as good box office. Goodman Ace printed this exact wording in “The Saturday Review” on 13 August 1955 — but he attributed it to George Jessel in the same breath, and Quote Investigator credits Jessel.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Strictly Screwball” by Katharine Brush, “The Washington Post” — dated 1941 in Quote Investigator’s prose and 8 March 1942 in its own citation

source.excerpt: They tell the story of George Jessel’s once passing a funeral home where a celebrity lay in state and the crowd waiting to file by for a last glimpse was four-deep. “You see,” said the veteran showman, “you give the people what they want and they’ll come.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s study of the quip ↗ transcribes Goodman Ace’s 13 August 1955 “Saturday Review” column and shows Ace crediting George Jessel in the same sentence. Its stated conclusion is that “George Jessel should be credited with this quip.”

The same page names the earliest instance it has found as a Katharine Brush column in “The Washington Post,” where Jessel’s line is truncated to “Give ’em what they want.” QI’s prose dates that column to 1941 while its own bibliographic note gives 8 March 1942 — we report both rather than choose, because we could not read the column itself.

QI documents the drift directly: the joke was later pinned on Goodman Ace ↗, Red Skelton and Groucho Marx, and the funeral was retrofitted to Harry Cohn ↗ (d. 1958) and Louis B. Mayer ↗ (d. 1957) — both of whom died after the line was already in print.
Jessel’s life dates are confirmed against his Wikipedia entry ↗ (3 April 1898 – 23 May 1981).
source.excerptNote: Goodman Ace’s column of 13 August 1955, as transcribed by Quote Investigator. The words inside the quotation marks are Jessel’s; the framing is Ace’s.

author.name: George Jessel
author.heading: About George Jessel
author.metaLine: 1898–1981 · American vaudeville comedian, actor and toastmaster
author.bio: George Jessel was a vaudeville headliner who became one of American show business’s most reliable after-dinner speakers — so reliable that he was nicknamed the “Toastmaster General of the United States.” He starred in the stage version of The Jazz Singer and spent six decades as a performer, producer and professional wit. Jokes of exactly this kind were his stock in trade, which is part of why so many of them later drifted to better-remembered names.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is a joke with an unusually crowded field of claimants. Quote Investigator lists six humorists and two funerals, and the only name with a contemporaneous paper trail is the one the joke is rarely told under.

items.why: Ace printed this exact wording in “The Saturday Review” on 13 August 1955 and in his book “The Book of Little Knowledge” the same year — but in both cases he credited George Jessel ↗. Being the first to print a line is not the same as writing it.

A 1967 biography of Harry Cohn reports Skelton delivering a version on television a few nights after Cohn’s 1958 funeral, and QI notes Skelton is “generally credited with the line” ↗ — thirteen years after Jessel’s version was in print.
Kenneth Tynan attributed a version to Groucho in “The Observer” in 1958, as QI documents ↗. That is three years after Ace’s printing and later still than the newspaper instance.
A 1969 Lahr biography and Bacon’s own 1976 memoir each claim the line, both recorded by QI ↗. Bacon’s account concedes the point neatly: “every joke is in the public domain.”

items.who: Harry Cohn and Louis B. Mayer
items.why: The joke is usually told over Cohn’s or Mayer’s coffin, but QI shows the quip in print before either man died ↗ — Mayer in 1957, Cohn in 1958. The mogul in the original telling is nameless.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗ is unambiguous: the quip belongs to George Jessel, and “the joke may have been retold when Harry Cohn died and when Louis B. Mayer died, but the remark was already in circulation.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line survives because it does two jobs at once. On the surface it is the oldest platitude in show business — give the audience what it wants and it will turn up. Aimed at a funeral, it becomes an obituary: the crowd is not mourning, it is enjoying the show.

That is also why it kept changing hands. A joke this portable attaches itself to whichever wit is most famous at the moment of retelling, and to whichever studio tyrant has most recently died. Quote Investigator’s chronology is really a record of a joke migrating upward through six comedians across thirty-five years.
detailsBody: The retrofitting is the interesting part. Jessel’s version, as printed in the 1940s and again by Goodman Ace in 1955, has a nameless celebrity. Only in 1961 does a humour anthology attach it to Louis B. Mayer, and only in 1963 does Budd Schulberg attach it to Harry Cohn — by which point the line had been circulating for roughly two decades.

Both attributions are chronologically impossible as origin stories: Mayer died in 1957 and Cohn in 1958, years after the joke was in print. The funerals did not produce the joke; the joke was waiting for them.
context.pull: The crowd is not mourning. It is enjoying the show.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator transcribes Goodman Ace’s 13 August 1955 Saturday Review column, in which Ace tells the funeral joke and credits George Jessel.
Quote Investigator states its conclusion that George Jessel should be credited with the quip, and that the remark was already circulating before Cohn’s and Mayer’s funerals.
George Jessel lived 3 April 1898 to 23 May 1981 and was an American entertainer.
Goodman Ace (1899–1982) was an American humorist, radio writer and magazine columnist.
Harry Cohn ran Columbia Pictures and died in 1958.
Louis B. Mayer was the MGM studio chief and died in 1957.
